sect1.title: Setting up Roundcube

para.emphasis: (Note: The following section assumes that roundcube v0.7 and MySQL community server have been installed, see )

sect1.para: We have finally come to the part that users will see; the Web-based mail client. To setup Roundcube do the following steps:

listitem.para: Extract the sources to your SSL enabled http document root. We also recommend to change the main directory name for Roundcube to something more generic, say "webmail". Using the structure suggested previously in this document this would then be ‘/srv/www/ssl-htdocs/webmail’ and will make it possible to access your mail in a natural way as "https://localhost/webmail/"

tip.para: One alternative way of placing Roundcube sources is outside the document root, say “/usr/local/share”. Then we create an Apache alias to that directory. This means that if the user accesses (for example) “/webmail” Apache knows that it should actually fetch the content from the directory “/usr/local/share/roundcube” assuming we have setup our aliases in that way. Please refer to the Apache documentation for more details on the alias command. This is a good practice to avoid installing Web-applications directly in the document root.

listitem.para: Make sure that the Web-server can write to ‘temp’ and ‘logs’ directories within the extracted files in the document root by executing the following command as root
Setup the MySQL user and database that roundcube should use as follows (this assumes that you previously have installed MySQL and have set a password for the root user.)
Note: You can change the user and password to something better but since the database is only accessible from localhost it is still quite secure.
Point your browser to the installer directory https://webmail/installer/
The installation is a three step process. The first step is a verification that the PHP5 installation has all necessary modules installed. Verify that all the necessary prerequisites are fulfilled.
In the next step the details of the database, the IMAP and SMTP settings must be given. Below are some examples on how this can be specified (change user and passwords according to your settings)

para.emphasis: Note: Make sure that auto_create_user is marked since it will be impossible to login otherwise!
Note: Please leave the SMTP username and password empty. Roundcube will then use the login information to access the SMTP user.

listitem.para: In the next step the installer will show the two configuration files "main.inc.php" and "db.inc.php". Download them and store them in the config directory.
The final step in the setup is a test to make sure that the settings are correct. Make sure that all these tests succeeds before proceeding!

Once Roundcube is working, you have a fully functional web-based interface to your mail. However, you'll likely also want to configure native mail clients on your devices (smartphones, tablets, desktop applications like Thunderbird or Mail.app). These clients connect directly to your Dovecot IMAP server (port 993 with SSL) and Postfix SMTP server (port 587 or 25 with STARTTLS) using the same username and password you use for Roundcube. The key advantage of IMAP is that all your devices stay synchronized - marking a message read on your phone will show it as read in Roundcube and on your desktop client.

Remember that your server certificates are self-signed, so when connecting your first client, you'll need to explicitly accept the certificate warning. This is expected behavior with self-signed certificates. Each client device will need to accept the certificate once. If you find the warnings bothersome, you can install your CA certificate on each device, or consider using Let's Encrypt certificates for a production deployment (though this wasn't common practice when this guide was written).

It should now be possible to point your browser to the directory where you have installed Roundcube (https://localhost/webmail/) and see the interface. After making sure that this works the installer directory should be removed.
